hero.title: ☠️ Poison Name Generator
hero.tagline: Poisons with names an assassin would use: Widow's Kiss, Hangman's Honey, the Quiet Guest.

article.intro: A good fictional poison has a name that sounds almost kind: the Quiet Guest, Gentle Death, Sleeper's Wine. This **poison name generator** gives you names for poisons in stories and games, with the form they come in and what they do. All of them are invented, for fiction only.

sections.heading: How real poisons got their names
sections.content:
• Belladonna is Italian for "beautiful lady": deadly nightshade drops were once used to widen the pupils, which was thought attractive.
  • Wolfsbane, or aconite, was said to have been used to poison wolves; folklore made it a guard against werewolves.
  • Hemlock is the poison Socrates was condemned to drink in Athens in 399 BC.
  • Arsenic was nicknamed "inheritance powder" in 19th-century France, for obvious reasons.

The pattern holds in fiction: the best poison names are euphemisms, beautiful on the outside.

sections.heading: Poisons in fiction and games
sections.content:
• Agatha Christie worked in a hospital dispensary during the First World War, and her knowledge of poisons shows in dozens of novels.
  • Game of Thrones has the Strangler and Tears of Lys: poisons with names as memorable as the people they kill.
  • D&D has its own, like Midnight Tears, which does nothing until midnight, and drow poison, which puts its victims to sleep. Give yours a name and a rule, and players will remember it.

sections.heading: Writing a poison
sections.content:
• The form matters. A poison in wine needs a feast; a poisoned candle needs a long night in a closed room.
  • The effect is a clue. A poison that "looks like old age" is a mystery plot. One that leaves the victim hearing everything is a horror one.
  • Every poisoner needs a name too. Try the Assassin Name Generator.

faqs.question: Are these real poisons?
faqs.answer: No. The names, forms and effects are invented for stories and games. The article mentions a few real ones only for the history of their names.

faqs.question: What makes a good poison name?
faqs.answer: Something gentle with a sting in it: a euphemism like Widow's Kiss or the Quiet Guest is creepier than anything with 'death' in it twice.

faqs.question: Can I use these in D&D or a story?
faqs.answer: Yes, they're free to use and you don't need to credit the site.
